passage:
Dear Dilnaz,
You asked how I stayed so calm last week. Honestly, I wasn't calm, I was curious about how little I cared. A stranger kept replying under my cooking videos with the same insult, only to watch me react. Old me would have typed a paragraph. This time I muted, blocked, and went to make tea. The next day a different person wrote, politely, that my rice timings were off for old cookers. That one I answered, with thanks. Ignoring the first wasn't weakness; it kept my evenings mine. The troll got nothing from me, and I had forgotten the name by dinner 🙂
Come on Sunday and taste the corrected rice.
Zeenat

qa.q: Which stranger did Zeenat answer, and what had that person pointed out?
qa.a: Zeenat answered the one who wrote, politely, that the rice timings were off for old cookers, and replied with thanks.

qa.q: What does Zeenat mean by saying that ignoring the first stranger wasn't weakness?
qa.a: Zeenat sees ignoring the troll as protection. It kept the evenings calm and gave the person who only wanted a reaction nothing.

qa.q: How can Dilnaz tell which comments deserve a reply?
qa.a: Answer people who criticise in good faith, like the rice-timing comment, and mute or block those who only want a reaction.

qa.q: What was the troll probably after, and what happened instead?
qa.a: They wanted to watch Zeenat react and get attention. After the mute and block they got no reaction at all.

grounding: A troll provokes for attention; not feeding them by muting and blocking is protection, while good-faith criticism gets an answer.

passage:
Tuesday. Dilnaz's baking videos had eight thousand followers, and one of them, a user called Nitin_Truth, had commented on every post for a month: "Fake oven." "Nobody eats this." "Talentless." Tonight she spent an hour writing a clever reply. Her tea went cold.

Thursday. She read her reply again and deleted it. He wanted exactly this, her attention. She muted him, then blocked him. Her thumb shook a little, but it felt like shutting a noisy window.

Sunday. A new comment arrived from someone else: "Your sponge sank in the middle, like mine. Too much baking powder?" Dilnaz watched the clip again. The commenter was right.

She replied warmly, thanked them, and filmed a short fix for the next video. It got more likes than anything she'd posted. She didn't think about Nitin_Truth once that day.

qa.q: What did Nitin_Truth comment on Dilnaz's posts?
What did Dilnaz feel when she muted and blocked the troll?
qa.a: She felt nervous, her thumb shaking a little, but also relieved, like shutting a noisy window.

qa.q: Which choice worked better for Dilnaz, and why?
qa.a: Ignoring the troll and engaging with the good-faith comment about the sponge, because it gave her useful help instead of feeding someone who only wanted a reaction.

qa.q: How might the commenter about the sunken sponge see Dilnaz's reply?
qa.a: They would likely feel appreciated and heard, since Dilnaz thanked them and even filmed a fix based on their tip.

grounding: Across several days, the passage shows someone learning to mute and block a troll who only wants a reaction while engaging with a good-faith critic.

passage:
"Disha, you keep refreshing that comment. Stop a minute. Your old uncle has a story.

Back when the internet was new, I, Samir, was twenty-three and wrote match reports for a cricket forum. There was one fellow, called himself Bouncer99. Every report, he'd write that I knew nothing, that my English was a joke. I stayed up nights writing long replies. He loved it. He'd come back with ten more.

Then a senior member messaged me: 'He's hungry. Stop feeding him.'

So I stopped. Didn't reply. Used the ignore button. Took a week before my fingers stopped itching.

Meanwhile a schoolteacher from Kanpur wrote that I'd got a scorecard wrong. I checked; she was right. I thanked her, fixed it, and we wrote to each other for years.

Ignore the hungry ones, beta. Answer the ones who actually want to talk."

qa.q: What was the name of the forum troll?
How did young Samir feel during the week after he stopped replying?
qa.a: He felt restless and itchy to reply, even though he knew answering only fed the troll.

qa.q: Which choice in the story turned things around?
qa.a: Taking the senior member's advice to stop replying and use the ignore button, while still thanking the teacher who fixed a real mistake.

qa.q: How might the schoolteacher from Kanpur have seen Samir's response?
qa.a: She likely felt respected, since he thanked her and fixed the error, which led to years of friendly letters.

grounding: An elder recalls learning to ignore a troll who wanted a reaction while engaging warmly with a good-faith critic.
